When $A$ and $B$ are **disjoint** (mutually exclusive) the intersection is empty, the correction term is $0$, and the rule simplifies to $P(A \cup B) = P(A) + P(B)$. That simplification is a special case, never the default.

This is inclusion-exclusion again, weighted by probability instead of raw counts. A cheap sanity check comes with it: probabilities never exceed $1$, so if adding two of them takes you past $1$ you have certainly dropped a correction term.
sections.code:
Draw one card from a standard 52-card deck. All 52 outcomes equally likely.

   H = "the card is a heart"        |H| = 13
   F = "the card is a face card"    |F| = 12   (J, Q, K in four suits)
   H and F together = {J-heart, Q-heart, K-heart}   |H and F| = 3

Naive addition double-counts those three cards:
   13 + 12 = 25, but only 22 distinct cards are a heart or a face card.

Addition rule (inclusion-exclusion for two events):
   P(H or F) = P(H) + P(F) - P(H and F)
             = 13/52 + 12/52 - 3/52
             = 22/52 = 11/26

Special case - disjoint events. Let T = "the card is a spade".
   H and T is impossible, so P(H and T) = 0 and the correction vanishes:
   P(H or T) = 13/52 + 13/52 = 26/52 = 1/2

annotations.text: 13 + 12 = 25 counts the three heart face cards in both totals; the correction removes exactly one copy of each.
Subtract the intersection once, not twice - afterwards every qualifying card is counted exactly once.
Disjoint is a property of the events, not a convenience: a card cannot be a heart and a spade, so the term is genuinely zero.

checkpoint.prompt: Roll two fair dice. Let $D =$ "both dice show the same number" and $T =$ "the sum is at least 10". Work through $P(D \cup T)$. Give the first three as fractions over 36, and the last in lowest terms.
checkpoint.explain: Only $(5,5)$ and $(6,6)$ satisfy both events, so the naive $12/36$ overcounts by exactly those two outcomes. Dropping the correction here inflates the answer by a fifth - large enough to matter, small enough to look plausible.

sections.title: Conditioning, the Multiplication Rule, and Independence
sections.body:
**Conditional probability** is a new sample space rather than a new formula: learning that $B$ occurred deletes every outcome outside $B$ and rescales what is left, giving $$P(A \mid B) = \frac{P(A \cap B)}{P(B)}, \qquad P(B) > 0.$$

Multiplying through yields the **multiplication rule** $P(A \cap B) = P(B)\,P(A \mid B)$, which is how sequential experiments are computed - drawing without replacement, one stage at a time.

$A$ and $B$ are **independent** exactly when $P(A \cap B) = P(A)P(B)$, equivalently when $P(A \mid B) = P(A)$: knowing $B$ tells you nothing about $A$. Independence is an arithmetic coincidence you must verify, never something to assume because two events feel unrelated - and it is not disjointness, since disjoint events of positive probability are as **dependent** as events get.
sections.code:
Two dice again. Condition on C = "the red die shows an even number".

Unconditional:  P(sum = 8) = 5/36     {(2,6),(3,5),(4,4),(5,3),(6,2)}

Conditioning throws away every outcome outside C and renormalises:
   |C| = 18 outcomes survive (red in {2,4,6}, blue anything)
   of those, sum = 8 happens for (2,6), (4,4), (6,2)  ->  3 outcomes

   P(sum = 8 | C) = P(sum = 8 and C) / P(C) = (3/36) / (18/36) = 3/18 = 1/6

Multiplication rule, read right to left: P(A and B) = P(B) * P(A | B)
   Two cards, no replacement:  P(both aces) = (4/52) * (3/51) = 1/221

Independence test - compare P(A and B) against P(A) * P(B):
   A = "red die is 3", D = "sum is 7":  1/36  vs  (1/6)(1/6) = 1/36   INDEPENDENT
   A = "red die is 3", E = "sum is 8":  1/36  vs  (1/6)(5/36) = 5/216 DEPENDENT

annotations.text: The denominator moved from 36 to 18 - conditioning is renormalisation, which is why P(A | B) may be larger or smaller than P(A).
The 3/51 already assumes the first ace is gone; that is the conditional factor doing its job.
Same event A, two different partners, two different verdicts - independence is a property of the pair, never of one event alone.

checkpoint.prompt: Roll one fair die. $A =$ "the roll is even" and $B =$ "the roll is at most 2". Complete the independence test: fractions in lowest terms, and the verdict as one word (independent or dependent).
checkpoint.template:
P(A) = 1/2      P(B) = 1/3
A and B = {2}, so P(A and B) = ___
P(A) * P(B) = ___
Verdict: A and B are ___
checkpoint.explain: The two sides agree, so the events are independent even though both describe the very same roll - independence lives in the arithmetic, not in causal separation. Widen $B$ to "at most 3" and the identical physical setup now fails the test.

sections.title: Bayes Theorem and the Base-Rate Trap
sections.body:
Writing $P(A \cap B)$ two ways and equating them gives **Bayes theorem**, the rule for reversing a conditional: $$P(A \mid B) = \frac{P(B \mid A)\,P(A)}{P(B)}.$$

The denominator is normally rebuilt with the **law of total probability**, $P(B) = P(B \mid A)P(A) + P(B \mid \overline{A})P(\overline{A})$ - the addition rule applied to the two disjoint ways $B$ can happen.

Now the famous trap. A 99% accurate test for a disease affecting 1 person in 1000 returns a positive result that is wrong about **95% of the time**. Nothing is broken: the healthy group is 999 times larger, so its small false-positive rate still produces twenty times more positives than the tiny sick group does.

The **base rate** $P(A)$ multiplies the whole numerator, and ignoring it is the most common probability error made outside a classroom.
sections.code:
A disease affects 1 person in 1000. The test has 99% sensitivity
(a sick person tests positive 99% of the time) and 98% specificity
(a healthy person tests negative 98% of the time, so 2% false positives).

Imagine 100,000 people and just count them.

                     test +      test -        total
   has disease           99           1           100
   healthy            1,998      97,902        99,900
                    -------                  --------
   total +            2,097                   100,000

   P(disease | test +) = 99 / 2097 = 11/233 = 4.7%

The same numbers through Bayes theorem:

   P(D | +) = P(+ | D) P(D) / [ P(+ | D) P(D) + P(+ | not D) P(not D) ]
            = (0.99)(0.001) / [ (0.99)(0.001) + (0.02)(0.999) ]
            = 0.00099 / 0.02097 = 0.0472

The 1,998 false positives are drawn from a group 999 times larger than
the sick group. That size ratio - the base rate - beats the 99% accuracy.

annotations.text: 100 sick people, 99 of whom test positive - the sensitivity is doing exactly what it promised.
2% of 99,900 is 1,998 false positives, twenty times the true positives. This row is the entire paradox.
Counting whole people is Bayes theorem with the denominators cleared - identical answer, far harder to get wrong.

checkpoint.prompt: A factory has two machines. Machine A makes 60% of the items and 2% of them are defective; machine B makes the other 40% and 5% of them are defective. An item is chosen at random and is defective. What is the probability it came from machine A? Show the law-of-total-probability denominator, and give the answer as a fraction in lowest terms.
checkpoint.explain: Machine A makes more items while B makes proportionally more defects, and those two pulls run in opposite directions - which is exactly why $3/8$ lands below A's $60\%$ share yet nowhere near zero. The denominator $0.012 + 0.020 = 0.032$ is the overall defect rate, and every Bayes problem is ultimately a fight over what belongs in that denominator.

guided-practice.prompt: Two fair dice are rolled. Complete the count for $A =$ "the sum is 7". Enter whole numbers in the first two blanks and fractions in lowest terms in the last two.
guided-practice.explain: Seven is the most likely total precisely because it has the most ordered pairs producing it - the probability follows the count, and the count follows the choice of $S$. The last blank is the complement rule saving you from enumerating thirty outcomes.
guided-practice.hint: The outcome is an ordered pair, so (3,4) and (4,3) are distinct members of $A$.

guided-practice.prompt: One card is drawn from a standard 52-card deck. Let $H =$ "heart" and $F =$ "face card (J, Q, K)". Walk the addition rule through to $P(H \cup F)$. Give the first three as fractions over 52 and the last in lowest terms.
guided-practice.explain: The jack, queen and king of hearts belong to both events, so adding $13 + 12$ counts them twice and the subtraction restores each to a single count. Twenty-two distinct cards over fifty-two reduces to $11/26$, which is comfortably below the $25/52$ the naive sum would claim.
guided-practice.hint: There are exactly three cards that are both a heart and a face card.

guided-practice.prompt: Two fair dice are rolled. Compute $P(\text{sum} = 8)$ and then $P(\text{sum} = 8 \mid \text{the first die is even})$. State how many outcomes survive the conditioning, give both probabilities as fractions in lowest terms, and say whether the evidence made the sum of 8 more or less likely.
guided-practice.explain: Conditioning shrank the sample space from 36 outcomes to 18 and kept 3 of the 5 favourable ones, so the ratio rose from $5/36$ to $3/18 = 1/6$. The lesson is that evidence is not automatically bad news for an event - it reweights, and the direction depends entirely on how much of the favourable set survives.
guided-practice.hint: The surviving outcomes are those with first die in $\{2,4,6\}$; among them find every pair summing to 8.

guided-practice.prompt: Two cards are drawn from a standard deck without replacement. Complete the multiplication-rule computation for "both cards are aces". Enter whole numbers in the first three blanks and a fraction in lowest terms in the last.
guided-practice.template:
P(first is an ace) = 4/___
P(second is an ace | first was an ace) = ___/___
P(both aces) = (4/52) * (3/51) = ___
guided-practice.explain: Both the numerator and the denominator drop by one because the first ace has left the deck - that shrinking denominator is exactly what makes the second factor conditional rather than independent. With replacement it would be $(4/52)^2 = 1/169$, a visibly larger number.
guided-practice.hint: After one ace is removed there are 3 aces left among 51 cards.

guided-practice.prompt: A classmate claims that because two events cannot both happen, they must be independent. Explain why mutually exclusive events with non-zero probabilities are in fact dependent, and give the test that settles the question.
guided-practice.explain: Disjointness makes $P(A \cap B) = 0$ while $P(A)P(B) > 0$, so the defining equation fails as loudly as it can - and intuitively, learning that $B$ happened tells you $A$ definitely did not, which is maximum information rather than none. The test is always the same: compare $P(A \cap B)$ with $P(A)P(B)$ and believe the arithmetic.
guided-practice.hint: What is $P(A \mid B)$ when $A$ and $B$ cannot both occur?

problem-set.prompt: An urn holds 5 red and 3 blue balls. Two are drawn without replacement. Compute (a) $P(\text{both red})$ and (b) $P(\text{the second ball is red})$, both as fractions in lowest terms. For (b), use the law of total probability over the colour of the first ball, and comment on the result.
problem-set.explain: Part (b) lands on $5/8$, exactly $P(\text{first is red})$ - unconditionally the second draw is as likely to be red as the first, because nothing has been observed to break the symmetry between positions. That is the standard shock of this problem: the draws are dependent, yet the marginal probabilities are identical.

problem-set.prompt: A family has two children, and each child is independently a boy or a girl with probability $\frac{1}{2}$. Given that at least one child is a boy, what is the probability that both are boys? Write out the sample space, state which outcomes the evidence eliminates, and give the answer as a fraction in lowest terms.
problem-set.explain: The evidence removes only GG, leaving three equally likely outcomes of which one is BB - the tempting answer $1/2$ silently assumes a specific child was named, which the phrase "at least one" never does. This is the cleanest demonstration that a conditional probability is decided by the surviving sample space, not by intuition about the other child.
problem-set.hint: List BB, BG, GB, GG and cross out what "at least one boy" forbids.

problem-set.prompt: Two fair dice are rolled. Let $A =$ "the first die shows 3", $D =$ "the sum is 7", $E =$ "the sum is 8". Decide whether $A$ and $D$ are independent, and whether $A$ and $E$ are independent. Show the product test with exact fractions for both pairs.
problem-set.explain: $A$ and $D$ pass because 7 is the one total reachable from every first-die value, so knowing the first die leaves the chance of a 7 at $1/6$; for a sum of 8 the first die matters, since a 1 makes it impossible. Independence therefore depends on the specific numbers, not on any general fact about "the first die" versus "the sum".
problem-set.hint: $P(D) = 6/36$ and $P(E) = 5/36$; both intersections with $A$ contain exactly one outcome.

problem-set.prompt: Put these steps in order to derive Bayes theorem from the definition of conditional probability, ending with the form whose denominator is expanded for computation.
fragments: Apply the same definition the other way round: $P(B \mid A) = \frac{P(A \cap B)}{P(A)}$, valid when $P(A) > 0$.
Conclude $P(A \mid B) = \frac{P(B \mid A)\,P(A)}{P(B)}$.
Start from the definition $P(A \mid B) = \frac{P(A \cap B)}{P(B)}$, valid when $P(B) > 0$.
Substitute that expression for $P(A \cap B)$ into the first equation.
Rearrange the second equation into $P(A \cap B) = P(B \mid A)\,P(A)$.
Expand the denominator by the law of total probability: $P(B) = P(B \mid A)P(A) + P(B \mid \overline{A})P(\overline{A})$.
problem-set.explain: Bayes theorem is not an extra axiom - it is the single quantity $P(A \cap B)$ written with two different denominators and the equation solved. Seeing that makes the final expansion feel inevitable: $P(B)$ is rarely given directly, so it must be rebuilt from the two disjoint routes to $B$.
problem-set.hint: Both conditional statements are about the same intersection.

problem-set.prompt: A disease affects 1 person in 1000. A test has 99% sensitivity and 98% specificity. A randomly chosen person tests positive. Compute $P(\text{disease} \mid \text{positive})$. Work with a population of 100,000: report the number of true positives, the number of false positives, and the final probability as a percentage rounded to one decimal place.
problem-set.explain: The 99 true positives are swamped by 1,998 false ones, so the posterior is $99/2097 \approx 4.7\%$ - a test that is right 99% of the time on the sick and 98% of the time on the healthy still yields a positive that is usually wrong. The reason is arithmetic, not a flaw in the test: a small error rate applied to a huge healthy population outproduces a large hit rate applied to a tiny sick one.
problem-set.hint: Of 100,000 people, 100 have the disease and 99,900 do not. Fill in both rows before dividing.

problem-set.prompt: Prove that if $A$ and $B$ are independent, then $A$ and $\overline{B}$ are also independent. Start by splitting $A$ into its part inside $B$ and its part outside $B$, and finish by showing $P(A \cap \overline{B}) = P(A)P(\overline{B})$.
problem-set.explain: The engine of the proof is that $A \cap B$ and $A \cap \overline{B}$ are disjoint and their union is $A$, so $P(A \cap \overline{B}) = P(A) - P(A)P(B) = P(A)(1 - P(B))$. That the factorisation survives complementation is what makes independence a usable structural assumption rather than a coincidence about one particular pair of events.
problem-set.hint: $P(A) = P(A \cap B) + P(A \cap \overline{B})$, and independence lets you replace the first term.

exam.prompt: In probability, what is a **sample space**?
choices: The set of all possible outcomes of the experiment
The subset of outcomes we are interested in
The most likely outcome of the experiment
The number of outcomes divided by the number of trials
exam.explain: The second option defines an event, which is a subset of the sample space - conflating the two is what produces the wrong denominator. Everything downstream, including every conditional probability, is computed relative to a sample space that must be pinned down first.

exam.prompt: Two events $A$ and $B$ are **independent** precisely when which condition holds?
choices: $P(A \cap B) = P(A)P(B)$
$P(A \cap B) = 0$
$P(A \cup B) = P(A) + P(B)$
exam.explain: Options two and three both describe mutually exclusive events, which are the opposite of independent whenever both probabilities are positive. Independence is a multiplicative statement about the intersection; disjointness is an additive statement about the union.

exam.prompt: Two fair dice are rolled. $A =$ "the sum is 7" and $B =$ "the first die shows 2". Complete the addition rule. Enter whole numbers only.
exam.explain: The single shared outcome $(2,5)$ is what separates the correct $11/36$ from the naive $12/36$ - one outcome, but it is the whole point of the rule. Every union computation should begin by asking which outcomes satisfy both events.

exam.prompt: Two fair dice are rolled. Order these steps into a correct complement-rule computation of $P(\text{at least one die shows a 6})$.
fragments: Count the complement: each die has 5 non-six faces, so $|\overline{A}| = 5 \times 5 = 25$.
Let $A =$ "at least one die shows a 6", so $\overline{A} =$ "neither die shows a 6".
Apply the complement rule: $P(A) = 1 - \frac{25}{36} = \frac{11}{36}$.
Fix the sample space: ordered pairs, so $|S| = 36$ equally likely outcomes.
Therefore $P(\overline{A}) = \frac{25}{36}$.
exam.explain: Counting $A$ directly invites the classic error $6 + 6 = 12$, which double-counts $(6,6)$; the complement has no overlap to worry about and needs one multiplication. "At least one" is almost always a signal to negate the event before counting anything.

exam.prompt: A disease affects 1% of a population. A test has 95% sensitivity and 90% specificity. Using a population of 10,000, trace the computation of $P(\text{disease} \mid \text{positive})$. Give whole numbers for the counts and a fraction in lowest terms for the final step.
exam.explain: At roughly $8.8\%$ the posterior is nine times the $1\%$ base rate yet still far from a diagnosis - the evidence moved the belief a long way without moving it past doubt. Notice the false positives (990) outnumber the true ones (95) even though the disease is ten times more common here than in the lesson's example.
exam.hint: Build both rows of the 2x2 table before dividing anything.

exam.prompt: A spam filter knows that 40% of incoming email is spam. The word "lottery" appears in 5% of spam messages and in 0.1% of legitimate messages. A message contains the word "lottery". Compute the probability it is spam: show the law-of-total-probability denominator as a decimal, and give the answer as a fraction in lowest terms and as a percentage to one decimal place.
exam.explain: The prior of $0.4$ is unremarkable, but the likelihood ratio is $50{:}1$, and that ratio is what drags the posterior to $97.1\%$. Set beside the medical test - same theorem, opposite conclusion - it shows the posterior is decided by base rate and likelihood ratio together, never by either one alone.

exam.prompt: Urn A holds 2 red and 3 blue balls; urn B holds 4 red and 1 blue ball. An urn is chosen by a fair coin flip and one ball is drawn from it. The ball is red. Compute $P(\text{urn A} \mid \text{red})$. Give $P(\text{red})$ and the final answer as fractions in lowest terms.
exam.explain: The prior was an even $1/2$ and the red ball pushed it down to $1/3$, because urn B produces red balls twice as often - evidence shifts belief in proportion to how much better one hypothesis explains it. The denominator $3/5$ is the overall chance of red, assembled from the two disjoint routes to a red ball.

exam.prompt: Three fair coins are flipped. Given that at least one coin came up heads, what is the probability that exactly two came up heads? Give the size of the conditioned sample space and the answer as a fraction in lowest terms.
exam.explain: The evidence deletes exactly one of the eight outcomes, TTT, so the denominator becomes 7 while the favourable count stays at 3 - the answer $3/7$ is slightly above the unconditional $3/8$. Whenever the evidence removes only unfavourable outcomes, the conditional probability must rise.
exam.hint: Only TTT is eliminated; three outcomes have exactly two heads.

exam.prompt: Let $S$ be a finite sample space of equally likely outcomes and let $A, B \subseteq S$. Prove the addition rule $P(A \cup B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(A \cap B)$ by a counting argument, and state what the rule reduces to when $A \cap B = \emptyset$.
exam.explain: The proof is inclusion-exclusion divided through by $|S|$: an outcome in both events contributes to $|A|$ and to $|B|$, so subtracting $|A \cap B|$ once leaves every outcome of the union counted exactly once. Because the argument is about counting, it needs the equally likely assumption to be a statement about probability at all.
exam.hint: Count the contribution of a single outcome to $|A| + |B|$ in each of the three possible cases.

exam.prompt: A newspaper reports that a screening test is "99% accurate", and concludes that a person who tests positive almost certainly has the condition. Explain what the report gets wrong, and what extra number a reader needs before the conclusion can be judged.
exam.explain: "99% accurate" reports $P(+ \mid \text{disease})$, while the reader wants $P(\text{disease} \mid +)$, and the two differ by the base rate - which is the missing number. When the condition is rare the healthy group is so much larger that its false positives dominate the positive column, so the posterior can sit in the low single digits despite the headline accuracy.

sections.title: Divisibility and the Division Algorithm
sections.body:
For integers $a$ and $b$ with $a \neq 0$ we write $a \mid b$ - read **$a$ divides $b$** - when there is an integer $k$ with $b = ak$. Everything on this floor rests on that one existential: to prove $a \mid b$ you must exhibit the integer $k$, and once you know $a \mid b$ you may name it.

The **division algorithm** says that for any integer $a$ and any $n > 0$ there are unique integers $q$ and $r$ with $a = nq + r$ and $0 \le r < n$. Uniqueness is exactly what makes $a \bmod n$ a well-defined value rather than a choice.

The remainder is never negative, even when $a$ is: $-47 = 8 \cdot (-6) + 1$, so $-47 \bmod 8 = 1$, not $-7$. The lemma you will reach for most often is **linearity**: if $d \mid a$ and $d \mid b$ then $d \mid ax + by$ for every choice of integers $x$ and $y$.
sections.code:
Divisibility:   a | b   means   b = a*k  for some integer k

  3 | 12      because  12 = 3*4         (k = 4)
  7 | 0       because   0 = 7*0         (k = 0)
  3 does not divide 10:  10 = 3*3 + 1,  remainder 1

Division algorithm:  a = n*q + r   with   0 <= r < n

  a =   47, n = 8 :   47 = 8*(  5) + 7      q =   5,  r = 7
  a =  -47, n = 8 :  -47 = 8*( -6) + 1      q =  -6,  r = 1
  a = -100, n = 7 : -100 = 7*(-15) + 5      q = -15,  r = 5
  a =   24, n = 8 :   24 = 8*(  3) + 0      q =   3,  r = 0   so 8 | 24

Why q = -6 and not -5 when a = -47:
  8*(-5) = -40  ->  r = -47 - (-40) = -7    rejected: r < 0
  8*(-6) = -48  ->  r = -47 - (-48) =  1    accepted: 0 <= 1 < 8

Linearity, the workhorse lemma:
  if d | a and d | b then d | (a*x + b*y) for all integers x, y

  d | a  gives  a = d*s
  d | b  gives  b = d*t
  a*x + b*y = d*s*x + d*t*y = d*(s*x + t*y)     an integer multiple of d

annotations.text: The quotient is pushed down rather than truncated toward zero, precisely so the remainder can stay in the range from 0 up to n.
Every later result - Bezout, inverses, Euclid's proof - is this one lemma applied to a cleverly chosen x and y.

checkpoint.prompt: Prove, working only from the definition of divisibility, that if $d \mid a$ and $d \mid a + b$ then $d \mid b$. Your argument must end by exhibiting the integer $k$ for which $b = dk$.
checkpoint.explain: The content of the argument is that divisibility survives subtraction as well as addition: $b = (a+b) - a = dm - ds = d(m-s)$, and $m - s$ is an integer because the integers are closed under subtraction. That closure is the only reason the Euclidean algorithm will later be allowed to replace a pair by a smaller one.

sections.title: Congruence and Its Arithmetic
sections.body:
$a \equiv b \pmod n$ means $n \mid a - b$, equivalently that $a$ and $b$ leave the same remainder on division by $n$. It is an equivalence relation, and better than that it is **compatible with addition and multiplication**: if $a \equiv b$ and $c \equiv d \pmod n$ then $a + c \equiv b + d$ and $ac \equiv bd \pmod n$.

That compatibility is a licence to replace any number by its remainder at any point in a calculation, which is what keeps the numbers small. Powers therefore cycle: modulo $7$ the powers of $3$ run $3, 2, 6, 4, 5, 1$ and then repeat, so from $1000 = 6 \cdot 166 + 4$ we get $3^{1000} \equiv 3^4 \equiv 4 \pmod 7$.

**Division is the operation that does not come free.** From $2 \cdot 3 \equiv 2 \cdot 6 \pmod 6$ you may not conclude $3 \equiv 6 \pmod 6$, because $\gcd(2,6) \neq 1$.
sections.code:
a = b (mod n)   means   n | (a - b)

  17 =  5 (mod 6)   because  6 | 12
  -4 =  3 (mod 7)   because  7 | -7
 100 =  0 (mod 4)   because  4 | 100

What survives:  if a = b and c = d (mod n) then
  a + c = b + d (mod n)        a * c = b * d (mod n)

So reduce as you go - 17 * 23 (mod 6):
  17 = 5 (mod 6),  23 = 5 (mod 6)
  17*23 = 5*5 = 25 = 1 (mod 6)          check: 391 = 6*65 + 1

Powers cycle. Powers of 3 modulo 7:
  k      1   2   3   4   5   6   7   8
  3^k    3   2   6   4   5   1   3   2      cycle length 6

  1000 = 6*166 + 4    so   3^1000 = 3^4 = 4 (mod 7)

What does NOT survive - cancellation:
  2*3 = 0 (mod 6)  and  2*6 = 0 (mod 6),  so 2*3 = 2*6 (mod 6)
  but 3 is not congruent to 6 (mod 6).  The culprit: gcd(2,6) = 2, not 1.

annotations.text: Reducing the factors before multiplying is legal only because congruence respects multiplication - it is the whole reason modular exponentiation is cheap.
The exponent is reduced modulo the cycle length, not modulo the modulus. Reducing 1000 modulo 7 here would be a different and wrong calculation.

checkpoint.prompt: Find the remainder when $2^{50}$ is divided by $7$. Show the cycle of powers you used and how you located $50$ inside it.
checkpoint.explain: The powers of $2$ modulo $7$ are $2, 4, 1$ repeating with period $3$, and $50 = 3 \cdot 16 + 2$ lands on the second entry, so the remainder is $4$. Note that $2^{50}$ itself is never computed - the cycle comes from the first few powers and the position inside it comes from the division algorithm.

sections.title: The Euclidean Algorithm, Bezout, and Inverses
sections.body:
$\gcd(a,b)$ is the largest integer dividing both. The **Euclidean algorithm** computes it from a single fact - $\gcd(a,b) = \gcd(b, a \bmod b)$ - which holds because linearity makes the common divisors of $a$ and $b$ exactly the common divisors of $b$ and $a - qb$. Each step strictly shrinks the second entry, so the process reaches $0$, and $\gcd(g, 0) = g$.

Running those divisions backwards writes the gcd as an integer combination of the two inputs. That is **Bezout's identity**: there exist integers $x$ and $y$ with $ax + by = \gcd(a,b)$.

The payoff is inversion. If $\gcd(a,n) = 1$ then $ax + ny = 1$ for some integers $x, y$, so $ax \equiv 1 \pmod n$ and $x$ is the **modular inverse** of $a$. More generally $ax \equiv b \pmod n$ has a solution exactly when $\gcd(a,n) \mid b$.

annotations.text: The gcd is the last non-zero remainder, never the zero that stops the loop.
Every line stays in the form (something)**803 + (something)**154 - simplifying the arithmetic early destroys the coefficients you are extracting.
An inverse is just the Bezout coefficient of a read modulo n; a negative coefficient is normalised by adding n.

checkpoint.prompt: Find the inverse of $7$ modulo $26$ as a residue in $\{0, 1, \dots, 25\}$. State the Bezout combination you used and verify your answer.
checkpoint.explain: From $26 = 3 \cdot 7 + 5$, $7 = 1 \cdot 5 + 2$, $5 = 2 \cdot 2 + 1$, unwinding gives $1 = 15 \cdot 7 - 4 \cdot 26$, so the inverse is $15$ and the check $7 \cdot 15 = 105 = 4 \cdot 26 + 1$ is the definition itself. Existence was settled before any arithmetic began, by $\gcd(7,26) = 1$.

sections.title: Primes, Unique Factorisation, and Euclid's Proof
sections.body:
A **prime** is an integer $p > 1$ whose only positive divisors are $1$ and $p$. The **fundamental theorem of arithmetic** states that every integer $n > 1$ factors into primes in exactly one way up to the order of the factors: $2024 = 2^3 \cdot 11 \cdot 23$, and no other multiset of primes multiplies to $2024$.

Uniqueness is the tool, not the slogan. It turns divisibility into a comparison of exponents - $d \mid n$ precisely when each prime exponent in $d$ is at most the matching exponent in $n$ - so $2024$ has $(3+1)(1+1)(1+1) = 16$ positive divisors, counted without listing a single one.

**Euclid's proof** that the primes never run out: suppose $p_1, \dots, p_k$ were all of them, set $N = p_1 p_2 \cdots p_k + 1$, and observe that each $p_i$ leaves remainder $1$ in $N$. Yet $N > 1$ has a prime factor, which is therefore missing from the list - a contradiction.
sections.code:
Factor 2024 by trial division:
  2024 / 2 = 1012
  1012 / 2 =  506
   506 / 2 =  253
   253 / 11 =  23          (253 = 11*23)
    23 is prime
  2024 = 2^3 * 11 * 23

Divisor count straight off the exponents (3, 1, 1):
  (3+1)*(1+1)*(1+1) = 16
  1  2  4  8  11  22  44  88  23  46  92  184  253  506  1012  2024

Euclid's argument as a skeleton:
  assume   p1, p2, ..., pk  is EVERY prime
  build    N = p1*p2*...*pk + 1
  then     N leaves remainder 1 on division by each pi, so no pi divides N
  but      N > 1, so N has a prime factor q  (fundamental theorem)
  hence    q is a prime outside the list  ->  contradiction

The construction need not itself be prime:
  2*3*5*7*11*13 + 1 = 30031 = 59 * 509
  59 and 509 are both primes missing from the list, which is all the proof needs.

annotations.text: Adding one to each exponent counts the choices for that prime, including the choice of taking it zero times.
The contradiction is that the list was assumed complete, not that N is prime - N usually is not.
30031 = 59 * 509 is the standard warning: the proof produces a new prime factor, never a formula for primes.

checkpoint.prompt: Give the prime factorisation of $600$ and use it to count the positive divisors of $600$ without listing them.
checkpoint.explain: $600 = 2^3 \cdot 3 \cdot 5^2$, so a divisor is fixed by choosing an exponent for each prime independently: $4 \cdot 2 \cdot 3 = 24$. The counting rule is valid only because the fundamental theorem guarantees that two different exponent choices can never give the same number.

unseen-problems.prompt: Apply the division algorithm to $a = -100$ and $n = 7$: give the unique $q$ and $r$ with $-100 = 7q + r$ and $0 \le r < 7$. Then argue that no other pair of integers satisfies both conditions.
unseen-problems.explain: The answer is $q = -15$ and $r = 5$, since $7 \cdot (-15) = -105$ and $-105 + 5 = -100$; the tempting $q = -14$ leaves $r = -2$, outside the permitted range. Uniqueness follows because two representations would give $7(q_1 - q_2) = r_2 - r_1$, forcing $7$ to divide a difference that lies strictly between $-7$ and $7$, and only $0$ qualifies.

unseen-problems.prompt: Prove that $6 \mid n^3 - n$ for every integer $n$. Factor first, then argue divisibility by $2$ and by $3$ separately from the fact that the factors are consecutive integers, and say why the two conclusions may be combined.
unseen-problems.explain: $n^3 - n = (n-1)n(n+1)$ is a product of three consecutive integers, so at least one is even and exactly one is a multiple of $3$. Combining the two into divisibility by $6$ needs $2$ and $3$ to be coprime - divisibility by $2$ and by $4$ would not combine into divisibility by $8$, so the coprimality is load-bearing rather than decorative.

unseen-problems.prompt: Run the Euclidean algorithm on $1071$ and $462$, writing out every division line, then back-substitute to produce integers $x$ and $y$ with $1071x + 462y = \gcd(1071, 462)$. State the gcd and verify the combination arithmetically.
unseen-problems.explain: The divisions are $1071 = 2 \cdot 462 + 147$, $462 = 3 \cdot 147 + 21$, $147 = 7 \cdot 21 + 0$, so the gcd is the last non-zero remainder, $21$; unwinding gives $21 = 462 - 3 \cdot 147 = 462 - 3(1071 - 2 \cdot 462) = 7 \cdot 462 - 3 \cdot 1071$. The coefficients are not unique - adding $462/21 = 22$ to $x$ while subtracting $1071/21 = 51$ from $y$ gives another valid pair.

unseen-problems.prompt: Solve $35x \equiv 12 \pmod{78}$ completely: decide first whether a solution exists, then find every residue modulo $78$ that works. Justify why your list is complete.
unseen-problems.explain: $\gcd(35,78) = 1$, so $35$ is invertible and the solution is unique modulo $78$: the inverse is $29$, giving $x \equiv 29 \cdot 12 = 348 \equiv 36 \pmod{78}$, checked by $35 \cdot 36 = 1260 = 16 \cdot 78 + 12$. Invertibility is exactly what collapses the solution set to a single residue - with a non-trivial gcd there would be either none or several.

unseen-problems.prompt: Prove that if $\gcd(a,n) = 1$ then $a$ has a multiplicative inverse modulo $n$, and that the inverse is unique modulo $n$. Then prove the converse: if $a$ has an inverse modulo $n$ then $\gcd(a,n) = 1$.
unseen-problems.explain: Forwards, Bezout supplies $ax + ny = 1$ and reducing modulo $n$ kills the $ny$ term, leaving $ax \equiv 1$; uniqueness follows by multiplying $ax \equiv ax' \equiv 1$ through by an inverse. Backwards, $ax \equiv 1 \pmod n$ means $ax - 1 = nk$, so any common divisor of $a$ and $n$ divides $1$ - the same identity read in the other direction, which is why the two conditions are genuinely equivalent rather than merely related.

unseen-problems.prompt: Prove by contradiction that there are infinitely many primes. State precisely which earlier result guarantees that the number you construct has a prime factor at all.
unseen-problems.explain: Assuming a finite list $p_1, \dots, p_k$, the number $N = p_1 \cdots p_k + 1$ leaves remainder $1$ under division by each $p_i$, so none of them divides it; the fundamental theorem of arithmetic then supplies a prime factor of $N$ outside the list. That appeal is the step most often skipped - without it nothing rules out $N$ having no prime factor whatsoever, and the contradiction never arrives.

exam.prompt: Which statement is the definition of $a \equiv b \pmod n$?
choices: $n \mid a - b$
$a \mid b - n$
$a$ and $b$ are both multiples of $n$
$a - b$ divides $n$
exam.explain: Congruence is a statement about the difference, not about either number separately, which is why $17 \equiv 5 \pmod 6$ holds although neither is a multiple of $6$. The 'same remainder' reading is equivalent, but the difference form is the one that makes the addition and multiplication rules easy to prove.

exam.prompt: Which statement is the fundamental theorem of arithmetic?
choices: Every integer $n > 1$ has at least one prime divisor.
Every integer $n > 1$ is a product of primes, and that product is unique up to the order of the factors.
There are infinitely many primes.
For all integers $a$ and $n > 0$ there are unique $q, r$ with $a = nq + r$ and $0 \le r < n$.
exam.explain: Existence of a factorisation is the easy half and is all the first option claims; the theorem's force is **uniqueness**, which is what licenses counting divisors from exponents and comparing two factorisations term by term. The last option is the division algorithm, a different uniqueness statement altogether.

exam.prompt: Complete the Euclidean algorithm on $252$ and $198$. Each blank is a single integer.
exam.explain: The gcd is the last non-zero remainder, $18$ - the zero on the final line is the stopping signal, not the answer. Each line feeds the previous divisor and remainder into the next, and it is that strict decrease in the remainder that guarantees the algorithm halts.

exam.prompt: Put the steps of Euclid's proof that there are infinitely many primes into a valid logical order.
fragments: since $N > 1$, the fundamental theorem gives $N$ a prime factor $q$
assume for contradiction that $p_1, p_2, \dots, p_k$ are all the primes there are
$q$ is a prime not on the list, contradicting the assumption that the list was complete
form the number $N = p_1 p_2 \cdots p_k + 1$
each $p_i$ divides $N - 1$, so dividing $N$ by $p_i$ leaves remainder $1$ and $p_i \nmid N$
exam.explain: The appeal to the fundamental theorem has to come after $N$ is built and before the contradiction is drawn, because the contradiction concerns $q$, not $N$. Establishing that no $p_i$ divides $N$ beforehand is what makes $q$ a new prime rather than merely an existing one.

exam.prompt: Evaluate $3^{1000} \bmod 7$ by finding the cycle of powers. Give each answer as a single integer.

steps.label: the remainder of $1000$ on division by that $k$

exam.explain: Once $3^6 \equiv 1 \pmod 7$, the powers repeat with period $6$, so only $1000 \bmod 6 = 4$ matters and $3^{1000} \equiv 3^4 = 81 \equiv 4 \pmod 7$. The exponent is reduced modulo the cycle length, never modulo the modulus - reducing $1000$ modulo $7$ would answer a different question.

exam.prompt: Find the last two digits of $7^{2024}$. Justify the reduction you use rather than asserting it.
exam.explain: The last two digits are the residue modulo $100$: the powers of $7$ run $7, 49, 43, 1$ and repeat with period $4$, and $2024 = 4 \cdot 506$ lands exactly on the $1$, so the answer is $01$. Reporting $1$ instead of $01$ loses the distinction between a residue and a two-digit ending, which is what the question asked for.

exam.prompt: Prove by induction on $k$ that if $a \equiv b \pmod n$ then $a^k \equiv b^k \pmod n$ for every integer $k \ge 1$.
exam.explain: The base case $k = 1$ is the hypothesis itself, and the inductive step multiplies the congruences $a^k \equiv b^k$ and $a \equiv b$ using the compatibility of congruence with multiplication. The entire proof is one repeated application of that closure rule, which is also why the analogous claim about congruent exponents is false.

exam.prompt: Give the prime factorisation of $2024$, then count its positive divisors and state how many of them are even. Justify the counting rule you use.
exam.explain: $2024 = 2^3 \cdot 11 \cdot 23$ gives $(3+1)(1+1)(1+1) = 16$ divisors; an even divisor needs at least one factor of $2$, leaving $3$ choices for that exponent instead of $4$, so $3 \cdot 2 \cdot 2 = 12$ are even. The product rule is sound only because unique factorisation makes distinct exponent tuples produce distinct numbers.

exam.prompt: A student claims Euclid's proof shows that $p_1 p_2 \cdots p_k + 1$ is always prime, citing $2 \cdot 3 + 1 = 7$ and $2 \cdot 3 \cdot 5 + 1 = 31$. Given that $2 \cdot 3 \cdot 5 \cdot 7 \cdot 11 \cdot 13 + 1 = 30031 = 59 \cdot 509$, say exactly which step the student has misread and why the proof still stands.
exam.explain: The proof concludes only that $N$ has a prime factor outside the assumed list, never that $N$ is itself prime; $59$ and $509$ are both such new primes, so $30031$ confirms the argument rather than damaging it. Under the proof's own assumption the list was everything, so a composite $N$ is not an uncovered case - it is a case the assumption has already forbidden.

exam.prompt: Prove that $\gcd(a, b) = \gcd(b, a - qb)$ for all integers $a, b, q$ with $b \neq 0$, by showing the two pairs have exactly the same set of common divisors. Then say why this makes the Euclidean algorithm terminate.
exam.explain: If $d \mid a$ and $d \mid b$ then $d \mid a - qb$ by linearity, and conversely $a = (a - qb) + qb$ recovers $a$ from the new pair - so the two sets of common divisors are equal and their greatest elements coincide. Termination is a separate argument: with $q$ chosen by the division algorithm the remainder is a non-negative integer strictly below $b$, and no such sequence can descend forever.

exam.prompt: Solve $9x \equiv 6 \pmod{15}$ completely. List every solution as a residue modulo $15$ and explain why there is more than one, unlike the invertible case.
exam.explain: $\gcd(9,15) = 3$ and $3 \mid 6$, so solutions exist and there are exactly three: dividing the congruence through by $3$ gives $3x \equiv 2 \pmod 5$, hence $x \equiv 4 \pmod 5$, that is $x \in \{4, 9, 14\}$ modulo $15$. Because $9$ is not invertible modulo $15$ the solution set cannot collapse to one residue - the gcd counts the solutions, and would have given none had it not divided $6$.

exam.prompt: Complete the back-substitution that turns the Euclidean algorithm on $17$ and $43$ into an inverse of $17$ modulo $43$. Each blank is a single integer, and the last is a residue in $\{0, 1, \dots, 42\}$.
exam.explain: The Bezout coefficient of $17$ is $-5$, and an inverse is reported as a residue, so $-5 + 43 = 38$, checked by $17 \cdot 38 = 646 = 43 \cdot 15 + 1$. Every line keeps the expression as a combination of $43$ and $17$; collapsing the arithmetic early would destroy exactly the coefficients being extracted.

sections.title: What the Trial Asks For
sections.body:
The Trial is **one unseen problem set of eight problems, ninety marks, ninety minutes** - one mark a minute, which is the only pacing rule you need. Nothing here is new material: every problem is assembled from the nine floors you have already cleared, but no problem announces which floor it came from.

Marks are for **argument**, not for the final number. A correct answer with no justification scores a fraction of a fully reasoned one, and a wrong final number reached by a clearly correct method keeps most of its marks - so write the method down even when the arithmetic collapses.

Write every answer as prose plus symbols: name the technique you are using, state what you assume, and end with the claim you set out to prove. If a problem has a numeric answer, put it on its own line so the self-check list at the bottom of the paper can confirm it.
sections.code:
THE TRIAL - 8 problems, 90 marks, 90 minutes

  #  topic                                 marks   target time
  1  sets, inclusion-exclusion                10       10 min
  2  propositional logic, truth tables         8        8 min
  3  proof technique: contraposition          12       12 min
     and contradiction
  4  induction on a summation formula         12       12 min
  5  number theory: gcd, inverses, powers     12       12 min
  6  relations and equivalence classes        10       10 min
  7  graphs: degrees and colouring            10       10 min
  8  counting and probability                 16       16 min
                                            -----      ------
                                               90       90 min

MARKING, per problem
  ~60%  a correct and complete argument
  ~25%  the right technique, named and set up
  ~15%  the final answer, stated explicitly

So: a named technique + a wrong number  >  a right number + silence.

annotations.text: One mark per minute. If a 10-mark problem has eaten 20 minutes, leave it and come back - the marks are not there any more.
The three-line marking split is why an abandoned problem should still carry a sentence naming the technique you would have used.

checkpoint.prompt: Put the five parts of a written induction proof into the order a marker expects to read them.
fragments: State the proposition $P(n)$ precisely, and say which $n$ it ranges over.
Base case: verify $P(1)$ by direct computation.
Inductive hypothesis: assume $P(k)$ holds for an arbitrary fixed $k \ge 1$.
Inductive step: derive $P(k+1)$, marking the line where the hypothesis is used.
Conclude: by the principle of induction, $P(n)$ holds for all $n \ge 1$.
checkpoint.explain: The order is not decoration - it is what makes the argument checkable. The hypothesis has to be stated before the step that consumes it, or a reader cannot tell whether you assumed $P(k)$ or quietly assumed $P(k+1)$, which is the commonest way an induction proof silently begs the question.

sections.title: Choosing the Shape of the Argument
sections.body:
Most lost marks in a timed paper are not arithmetic - they are three minutes spent pushing a **direct proof** at a claim whose hypothesis is useless. The shape of the claim tells you the shape of the proof, and there are only five shapes worth reaching for.

A universal claim over $\mathbb{N}$ invites **induction**. An implication whose conclusion is easier to negate than its hypothesis is to use invites **contraposition**, since $P \Rightarrow Q$ and $\neg Q \Rightarrow \neg P$ are the same statement. A claim that no object exists invites **contradiction**: assume one does and derive an impossibility.

Two more: a claim of the form $\forall x,\ P(x)$ is destroyed by a single **counterexample**, and a claim that two finite sets have equal size is often cleanest as a **bijection**. Pick the shape in the first thirty seconds, write its name down, and the rest of the problem becomes bookkeeping.
sections.code:
PICKING THE SHAPE - read the claim, not the topic

  claim looks like                          reach for
  ----------------------------------------  --------------------
  for all n >= 1, P(n)                      induction
  P => Q, and ~Q is the easy end to hold    contraposition
  no x has property P / x is irrational     contradiction
  for all x, P(x)   (and you doubt it)      one counterexample
  |A| = |B|, both finite                    a bijection A -> B

WORKED: for every integer n, if n^2 is even then n is even.

  direct:          n^2 = 2k  =>  n = sqrt(2k)   ... stuck, no integers here
  contrapositive:  if n is odd then n^2 is odd
                   n = 2m + 1
                   n^2 = 4m^2 + 4m + 1 = 2(2m^2 + 2m) + 1   -> odd
                   done, and it took three lines

The two statements are logically identical, so proving the second
proves the first. Nothing was lost by turning the claim around.

annotations.text: The direct attempt fails for a structural reason: an even square hands you a square root, and square roots leave the integers. That is the signal to turn the claim around.
Odd is a constructive hypothesis - it hands you the witness $m$ immediately. That is almost always why the contrapositive is the easier direction.

checkpoint.prompt: Complete the technique-selection table. One word per blank, drawn from: induction, contrapositive, contradiction, counterexample.
checkpoint.template:
for all $n \ge 1$, $P(n)$   ->   prove by ___
$P \Rightarrow Q$, with $\neg Q$ the easier end to grab   ->   prove the ___
no object with the stated property exists   ->   prove by ___
the claim $\forall x,\ P(x)$ is false   ->   exhibit one ___
checkpoint.explain: Contraposition and contradiction get confused under time pressure because both open by negating something. The difference is what gets negated: contraposition negates only the conclusion and stays a direct argument, while contradiction negates the whole claim and must end at an explicit impossibility. If your contradiction never reaches an absurdity, it was a contrapositive all along.

sections.title: Checking an Answer You Cannot Run
sections.body:
Nothing executes in this dungeon, so **verification is a step you write, not a button you press**. Every closed form you derive can be tested against a small case in under a minute, and a formula that fails at $n = 1$ has just saved you the twelve marks you were about to lose.

The cheap checks are worth memorising. A probability must land in $[0, 1]$; a count must be a non-negative integer; a residue modulo $m$ must lie in $\{0, 1, \dots, m-1\}$; an inclusion-exclusion total can never exceed $|U|$; the edge count implied by a degree sum must come out whole.

When a check fails, the fastest repair is to re-derive the smallest case by hand rather than to re-read the algebra. Budget the last five minutes of the ninety for exactly this sweep across all eight answers.
sections.code:
VERIFY A CLOSED FORM BY TESTING SMALL n

claim:  sum_{i=1..n} i * 2^i  =  (n - 1) * 2^(n+1) + 2

  n = 1   left:  1*2                       = 2
          right: (1-1) * 2^2 + 2 = 0 + 2   = 2      agree

  n = 2   left:  1*2 + 2*4                 = 10
          right: (2-1) * 2^3 + 2 = 8 + 2   = 10     agree

  n = 3   left:  1*2 + 2*4 + 3*8           = 34
          right: (3-1) * 2^4 + 2 = 32 + 2  = 34     agree

Two agreeing cases are not a proof. But one DISagreeing case is a
disproof, and it costs thirty seconds to look for.

CHEAP SANITY CHECKS
  probability in [0,1]      |  count is a non-negative integer
  residue mod m in [0,m-1]  |  |A u B u C| <= |U|
  sum of degrees is even    |  edges = (sum of degrees) / 2 is whole

annotations.text: $n = 1$ is where a mis-stated closed form fails first: an off-by-one in the exponent or the constant shows up immediately at the smallest input.
This asymmetry is the whole point. Testing cases can only refute, never confirm, so it belongs in front of the proof as a filter rather than in place of it.

checkpoint.prompt: Verify the closed form $\sum_{i=1}^{n} i \cdot 2^i = (n-1)2^{n+1} + 2$ at two small values of $n$. Give each value as a plain integer, and answer the last step with yes or no.

steps.label: the closed form at $n = 1$, that is $(1-1)2^{2} + 2$
the closed form at $n = 3$, that is $(3-1)2^{4} + 2$
has the formula survived both tests? (yes / no)

checkpoint.explain: Agreement at $n = 1$ and $n = 3$ establishes nothing about $n = 40$, since infinitely many false formulas pass any finite sample. What the check buys is asymmetric: it cannot confirm the claim, but it can kill a mis-copied one before you spend twelve marks' worth of time inducting on it.

trial.prompt:
**THE TRIAL. Eight problems, 90 marks, 90 minutes.** Work in one continuous sitting, closed book. Answer every part in the one answer box, numbered `1(a)`, `1(b)`, and so on. Marks are for the argument: name your technique, state your assumptions, and put each numeric answer on its own line. The self-check list at the foot of the paper holds the required final answers - do not read it until you have finished.

**Problem 1 - Sets and inclusion-exclusion (10 marks).** Let $U = \{1, 2, \dots, 30\}$, and inside $U$ let $A$ be the multiples of $2$, $B$ the multiples of $3$, and $C$ the multiples of $5$.

- (a) Compute $|A \cup B \cup C|$ by inclusion-exclusion, showing all seven terms.
- (b) Hence compute $|\overline{A \cup B \cup C}|$, the number of elements of $U$ divisible by none of $2$, $3$, $5$.
- (c) In one sentence, say why $|A \cap B| = 5$ is obtained by counting multiples of $6$ rather than by multiplying $|A|$ and $|B|$.

**Problem 2 - Propositional logic (8 marks).**

- (a) Prove by truth table that $(p \Rightarrow q) \land (\neg p \Rightarrow q) \equiv q$. Show all four rows.
- (b) Is $(p \Rightarrow q) \Rightarrow (q \Rightarrow p)$ a tautology? Answer yes or no, and justify with a single row of a truth table.

**Problem 3 - Proof technique (12 marks).**

- (a) Prove that for every integer $n$, if $n^2$ is even then $n$ is even. Name the technique before you use it.
- (b) Using part (a), prove that $\sqrt{2}$ is irrational. Your argument must say exactly where the assumption that the fraction is in lowest terms is contradicted.

**Problem 4 - Induction (12 marks).**

- (a) Prove by induction that for all $n \ge 1$, $$\sum_{i=1}^{n} i \cdot 2^i = (n-1)2^{n+1} + 2.$$ Mark clearly the line in which the inductive hypothesis is used.
- (b) State the value of the sum when $n = 10$.

**Problem 5 - Number theory (12 marks).**

- (a) Compute $7^{2026} \bmod 13$. Use the order of $7$ modulo $13$ rather than repeated squaring alone, and state what that order is.
- (b) Find the multiplicative inverse of $7$ modulo $13$, as the representative in $\{0, 1, \dots, 12\}$.
- (c) Solve $7x \equiv 5 \pmod{13}$ for the least non-negative $x$.
- (d) Compute $\gcd(252, 198)$ by the Euclidean algorithm, then find integers $s, t$ with $252s + 198t = \gcd(252, 198)$.

**Problem 6 - Relations (10 marks).** Define $R$ on $S = \{1, 2, \dots, 12\}$ by $a \mathbin{R} b$ if and only if $a \equiv b \pmod 4$.

- (a) Prove that $R$ is an equivalence relation, treating reflexivity, symmetry and transitivity separately.
- (b) State the number of equivalence classes and give one representative of each.
- (c) Compute $|R|$, the number of ordered pairs $(a, b) \in S \times S$ satisfying the relation, and explain the count rather than enumerating it.

**Problem 7 - Graphs (10 marks).**

- (a) A simple graph $G$ has $10$ vertices, every one of degree $3$. How many edges does $G$ have? Justify with the degree-sum identity.
- (b) Prove that in any simple graph the number of vertices of odd degree is even.
- (c) State the chromatic number of the cycle $C_5$, with one sentence for why that many colours suffice and one for why fewer do not.

**Problem 8 - Counting and probability (16 marks).**

- (a) How many bit strings of length $10$ contain exactly four $1$s? Give the binomial coefficient and its value.
- (b) How many bit strings of length $10$ contain at least eight $1$s?
- (c) Two fair six-sided dice are rolled. Given that at least one die shows a $5$, what is the probability that the two dice sum to $8$? Give an exact fraction in lowest terms and name the rule you used.
- (d) In one sentence, say why the answer to (c) differs from the unconditional probability that the sum is $8$.

**Self-check.** The tests below list the required final answer to each numeric part. They check arithmetic only - the marks live in the reasoning above them.
trial.explain:
The paper is built so that no problem can be answered by pattern-matching to a single floor. Problem 3(b) is unreachable without 3(a), which is itself a contraposition, so two proof shapes have to be nested rather than chosen between; 5(a) is hopeless by brute force and forces you to see that the order of $7$ modulo $13$ divides $12$ and then reduce the exponent $2026$ modulo that order; 6(c) is a counting question wearing a relations costume, and rewards reading four classes of three elements as $4 \cdot 3^2$ instead of enumerating $144$ pairs; 8(c) punishes the reflex answer $5/36$, because conditioning has already shrunk the sample space from $36$ outcomes to $11$. That is the real subject of the Trial: these topics were never separate, and competence is knowing which of them a problem is secretly about.

**Self-check.** Compare these against your own answers before
you read the discussion above again.

- Problem 1(a): |A u B u C| — **22**
- Problem 1(b): elements of 1..30 divisible by none of 2, 3, 5 — **8**
- Problem 2(b): is (p => q) => (q => p) a tautology? — **no**
- Problem 4(b): the value of the sum at n = 10 — **18434**
- Problem 5(a): 7^2026 mod 13 — **4**
- Problem 5(b): the inverse of 7 modulo 13 — **2**
- Problem 5(c): least non-negative solution of 7x = 5 (mod 13) — **10**
- Problem 5(d): gcd(252, 198) — **18**
- Problem 6(b): number of equivalence classes — **4**
- Problem 6(c): |R|, the number of ordered pairs — **36**
- Problem 7(a): edges of a 3-regular graph on 10 vertices — **15**
- Problem 7(c): chromatic number of C_5 — **3**
- Problem 8(a): bit strings of length 10 with exactly four 1s — **210**
- Problem 8(b): bit strings of length 10 with at least eight 1s — **56**
- Problem 8(c): P(sum = 8 | at least one 5), exact fraction — **2/11**
